props.subtitle: Write web app manuals that users can find, follow and trust
props.title: Technical Writing for Software Docs

bullets: Four kinds of docs: tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation, and why not to mix them
Task pages: goal titles, prerequisites, one action per step, bold UI labels, results
Plain language: short sentences, active voice, one term per concept, style guides and Vale
Review: subject-matter expert check, follow-every-step test, editorial review
what.definition: Technical writing for software docs is the craft of writing pages that help a specific reader do or understand one thing in a software product, clearly, accurately and consistently.
what.summary: Most bad manuals fail the same way: they describe the software instead of helping the reader. This topic covers choosing the right kind of page (Diátaxis), writing task pages whose steps actually work, plain language and style guides, and a review loop that proves the page is true before users see it.

why.impact: Teams that skip the craft grow the Wall-of-Text Wyrm: long pages that mix history, field tables and a vague 'then export it as needed', so users still can't finish their task.
why.summary: Every page users can't follow becomes a support ticket, a mistake in the real system, or a user who gives up.

categories.analogy: A driving lesson in an empty car park: the instructor picks the route and nothing can go badly wrong.
categories.description: A tutorial is learning-oriented: it guides a beginner through a safe, guaranteed-to-work lesson, like a driving lesson.
categories.details: The reader is new and wants to learn, not to get a job done. You, the author, choose the path, with a small project, a fixed set of sample data and every step spelled out, so it always works. Keep explanation to a minimum and link to it instead. Success means the learner finishes and feels 'I can do this'. Example: 'Your first expense claim in 10 minutes'.
inScope: Guided first projects with sample data
Every step spelled out, always works
outOfScope: Getting a specific real job done (how-to guide)
Background theory (explanation)
categories.primaryFocus: Building a beginner's confidence by doing
categories.subtitle: Learning-oriented · action + study
categories.title: Tutorial

categories.analogy: A recipe: it assumes you can already hold a knife, and gets you to the dish.
categories.description: A how-to guide is goal-oriented: it gives a competent user the steps to achieve one specific real-world goal.
categories.details: The reader already knows the basics and has a real job in front of them: 'Export last month's claims to Excel', 'Reset a user's password'. Give them the steps to that goal and nothing else. Don't teach basics, don't explain the architecture; assume they can adapt the steps to their own data. Most pages of a web app manual are how-to guides.
outOfScope: Teaching the basics from zero (tutorial)
Listing every field (reference)
categories.subtitle: Goal-oriented · action + work
categories.title: How-to Guide

categories.analogy: A dictionary: you don't read it cover to cover, you look up the one word you need.
categories.description: Reference is information-oriented: dry, complete, accurate descriptions of the product (fields, settings, limits) to look things up.
categories.details: The reader is in the middle of work and needs one fact: what does the 'Retention period' field accept? What's the file-size limit? Which roles can approve? Reference describes, completely and consistently, in the same structure for every item. It doesn't instruct or explain. Tables of fields, settings, error codes, permissions and keyboard shortcuts are typical.
outOfScope: Step-by-step instructions (how-to)
Opinions and reasons (explanation)
categories.primaryFocus: Accurate facts to look up while working
categories.subtitle: Information-oriented · cognition + work
categories.title: Reference

categories.analogy: An article about why a recipe works, the chemistry of browning, read in an armchair rather than at the stove.
categories.description: Explanation is understanding-oriented: it discusses why things work the way they do, background and design decisions.
categories.details: The reader steps back from the keyboard to understand: why do approvals go through two levels? How do workspaces and projects relate? What changed in the new permission model and why? Explanation can discuss alternatives and give opinions, and it's where concepts live. It's read away from the task, not during it.
inScope: Why the product works the way it does
outOfScope: Instructions for a task
categories.subtitle: Understanding-oriented · cognition + study
categories.title: Explanation

categories.analogy: A restaurant menu that interrupts the list of dishes with the chef's life story.
categories.description: Mixing types on one page (e.g. long background inside how-to steps) makes every reader wade through content meant for someone else.
categories.details: The classic 'everything page' starts with three paragraphs of history, teaches the basics, lists every field in a table halfway through the steps, and finally gets to the procedure. The expert who wants the steps must scroll past the lesson, and the beginner is lost in the reference table. Split it: a how-to page with just the steps that links to a reference page and an explanation page.
inScope: Splitting everything pages into typed pages
Linking between types instead of embedding
outOfScope: Duplicating the same content in several types
categories.primaryFocus: Each reader gets only what they came for
categories.subtitle: One page, one kind of reader need
categories.title: Don't Mix the Types

categories.analogy: Station names on a train map match the signs on the platform letter for letter.
categories.description: Write UI labels in bold, spelled and capitalised exactly as they appear on screen.
categories.details: Readers scan the page, then scan the screen for the same word. Bold makes the label stand out in the text, and exact spelling and capitalisation let them match it instantly. If the button says Save changes, write **Save changes**, not 'save' or 'the Save Changes button'. When the UI label changes in a release, the doc must change too.
inScope: Buttons, menu items, tabs, field names, page titles
outOfScope: Text the user types (see Input Formatting)
categories.primaryFocus: Instant matching between page and screen
categories.subtitle: **Save**, not "save" or 'the save button'
categories.title: Bold UI Labels, Exactly as Shown

categories.analogy: 'At the second traffic light, turn left', not 'turn left at the second traffic light', when there are lefts everywhere.
categories.description: State where before what: 'In the Settings pane, select Save' so the reader looks in the right place first.
categories.details: If the sentence says 'Select Save in the Settings pane', the reader may click the first Save they see, and there are often several. Putting the location first tells their eyes where to go before telling their hand what to do. The same applies to conditions: 'If you see an error, select Retry' rather than 'Select Retry if you see an error'.
inScope: Panes, dialogs, tabs, regions of the page
outOfScope: Multi-level menus (see Menu Paths)
categories.primaryFocus: Guiding the eye before the hand
categories.subtitle: Where, then what
categories.title: Location Before Action

categories.analogy: A folder path on your computer: Documents > Reports > 2026.
categories.description: Write menu paths with a > separator, e.g. File > Export > PDF.
categories.details: A menu path compresses several clicks into one readable line: **File** > **Export** > **PDF**. Each item stays bold, and the > shows the order. Use it for straightforward menu navigation; if something happens between the clicks, such as a dialog, write separate steps instead.
outOfScope: Steps where a dialog or choice happens in between
categories.subtitle: File > Export > PDF
categories.title: Menu Paths with >

categories.analogy: The difference between the label on a form and what you write in the box.
categories.description: Format text the user types, code and file names in monospace, separate from UI labels.
categories.details: Readers must be able to tell 'click this' from 'type this'. In the **Name** field, enter `Q3-budget`. The bold word is on the screen; the monospace word goes into it. Monospace also shows exact characters (spaces, dashes, capital letters) that matter when typing, and it's the standard for file names like `claims.xlsx` and commands.
inScope: Values to type, file names, code and commands
outOfScope: UI labels (these are bold)
categories.primaryFocus: Separating what you see from what you type
categories.subtitle: `monospace` for what users type
categories.title: Input Formatting

categories.analogy: A referee who uses the same whistle for the same foul every time.
categories.description: Pick device-neutral verbs such as 'select' and 'enter' (as the Microsoft style guide recommends) and use them consistently.
categories.details: Web apps are used with mouse, touch and keyboard, so 'click' doesn't fit everyone; the Microsoft style guide recommends 'select'. The Google developer style guide still uses 'click' for mouse actions. Either can work; what matters is choosing one set of verbs in your house style and using it the same way on every page, so readers don't wonder whether 'press', 'hit' and 'click' mean different things.
inScope: Recording the choice in the house style
outOfScope: Mixing 'click', 'press', 'hit' and 'tap' for the same action
categories.subtitle: select · enter · choose, used the same way everywhere

children.text: Aim for an average of about 15–20 words per sentence.
One idea per sentence; split sentences joined by 'and', 'which' or 'so that'.
Write 'Select Save', not 'The Save button should be selected'.
Active voice says who does what; 'you' speaks directly to the reader.
Put the most important word or condition at the start of the sentence or heading.
'Refunds over 5,000 baht need manager approval' beats 'Please note that, in accordance with policy, manager approval is needed for refunds over 5,000 baht'.
Pick 'workspace' and use it everywhere.
Switching between 'workspace', 'project' and 'space' makes readers think they are different things.
Plain, literal sentences without idioms or jokes translate better and are easier for non-native readers.
'This will hit the ground running' is hard to translate; 'You can start using it immediately' isn't.

categories.analogy: A big, well-thumbed dictionary for the whole office.
categories.description: The Microsoft Writing Style Guide is a free public guide covering voice, UI text and terms for software docs.
categories.details: It covers voice and tone, how to describe UI elements and interactions, grammar, punctuation and a large A–Z word list of software terms. It is a natural base for end-user manuals of web apps, and it's where the 'select' recommendation comes from.
inScope: Voice, UI text, grammar, word list
outOfScope: Your own product names and decisions (house style)
categories.subtitle: Free public guide for software docs
categories.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide

categories.analogy: The engineering handbook on the shelf next to the dictionary.
categories.description: The Google developer documentation style guide is a free public guide focused on developer and technical docs.
categories.details: It covers tone, formatting of code, commands and UI elements, procedures, API reference and a word list. It suits developer-facing documentation, such as APIs, SDKs and admin or integration guides for a web app.
outOfScope: Your own product names and decisions (house style)
categories.subtitle: Free public guide for developer docs
categories.title: Google Developer Documentation Style Guide

categories.analogy: House rules on the fridge; the law of the land covers the rest.
categories.description: A house style guide records only your own decisions (product names, terms, tone) and defers everything else to one public guide.
categories.details: Don't write a 50-page style guide from scratch. Say 'we follow the Microsoft Writing Style Guide, except:' and list your own decisions: product and feature names, the one term per concept ('workspace', never 'project'), your verbs ('select'), tone, and Thai/English choices. Short enough that people actually read it.
outOfScope: Re-writing rules the public guide already covers
categories.subtitle: Only your own decisions
categories.title: House Style Guide

categories.analogy: A spell-checker that has read your style guide.
categories.description: Vale is a prose linter that checks docs against style rules, including packages for the Microsoft and Google guides, and can run in CI.
categories.details: Vale reads your Markdown and flags passive voice, banned words, wrong product names, overly long sentences and more, based on rule packages such as Microsoft and Google plus your own house-style rules. Run it in the editor while writing and in CI on every pull request, so reviewers can focus on meaning instead of commas.
outOfScope: Checking whether the steps are correct (that needs a person)
categories.subtitle: Style rules checked automatically
categories.title: Vale Prose Linter

props.intro: Support gets 40 tickets a week saying 'I can't export my report'. The docs page 'Reporting' is 2,500 words: two paragraphs on why the reporting engine was rebuilt, a table of every report field, then one paragraph that ends '...and then export it as needed.' You're asked to fix it.

outcome.lesson: Right page type, a well-built task page and a review loop that includes following the steps: that's the whole craft.
outcome.verdict: The step test catches that Export moved into the ⋯ menu in the latest release. Fixed, published, and tickets drop to 3 a week.

outcome.lesson: Moving a vague paragraph doesn't make it followable. Split the types, then write real steps.
outcome.verdict: Slightly better, but the paragraph still says 'export it as needed' and people still get lost.

outcome.lesson: Readers need a prerequisite, one action per step and the result, not warmth alone.
outcome.verdict: Friendlier, but just as vague. Tickets barely drop.

outcome.lesson: Someone must follow every step in the real app or staging before publishing.
outcome.verdict: Tickets drop, then rise again: step 3 says 'Select Export' but Export moved into the ⋯ menu last release.

outcome.lesson: A linter checks style, not whether the page serves the reader's task. The problem here is page type and missing steps.
outcome.verdict: The page is now grammatically perfect, and the tickets keep coming.

terms.detailedDefinition: Created by Daniele Procida, it places content on two axes, action vs cognition and acquisition vs application, giving four page types with different jobs.
terms.shortDefinition: A framework that sorts docs into tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation.
terms.whyItMatters: Deciding the page type first prevents the everything page.

terms.detailedDefinition: Goal-oriented and action-focused, without teaching basics or explaining theory. Most pages of a web app manual.
terms.shortDefinition: Steps that get a competent user to one real goal.
terms.whyItMatters: It's what most users open the manual for.

terms.detailedDefinition: Fields, settings, limits, permissions and error codes, described consistently and without instructions.
terms.shortDefinition: Complete, accurate facts to look up while working.
terms.whyItMatters: It answers the one fact a user needs mid-task.

terms.detailedDefinition: A role or permission, data ready, or earlier setup, listed before the first step.
terms.shortDefinition: What must be true before step 1.
terms.whyItMatters: Without it, users fail halfway and don't know why.

terms.detailedDefinition: A documentation philosophy from 'The Nurnberg Funnel' (1990): users learn by doing, so docs should get them acting fast and help them recover from mistakes.
terms.shortDefinition: John Carroll's approach: act quickly, cut the unneeded, support error recovery.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the reason task pages are short and action-first.

terms.detailedDefinition: Short sentences, active voice, 'you', key information first, one term per concept, no idioms.
terms.shortDefinition: Writing that readers understand the first time they read it.
terms.whyItMatters: Readers skim while working; plain language survives skimming and translation.

terms.detailedDefinition: The opposite of passive voice ('Save should be selected'), which hides who acts.
terms.shortDefinition: The subject does the action: 'You select Save'.
terms.whyItMatters: Instructions must make clear who does what.

terms.detailedDefinition: Product names, terminology and exceptions, deferring everything else to e.g. the Microsoft Writing Style Guide.
terms.shortDefinition: Your team's own decisions on top of a public guide.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across writers without a 50-page rulebook.

terms.detailedDefinition: Checks Markdown against rule packages (Microsoft, Google, your own) in the editor and in CI.
terms.whyItMatters: Machines check the commas so reviewers can check the meaning.

terms.detailedDefinition: 206.835 − 1.015 × words per sentence − 84.6 × syllables per word. Higher is easier.
terms.shortDefinition: A readability score from sentence and word length.
terms.whyItMatters: A warning light for dense text, not proof of clarity.

terms.detailedDefinition: Usually a developer or product owner who does the technical review of a page.
terms.shortDefinition: The person who knows how the feature really works.
terms.whyItMatters: Writers describe; SMEs confirm it's true.
